title: Tools needed for smooth Subaru head gasket job
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content:
Replacing head gaskets on an EJ25 engine, specifically in a 1998 Legacy Outback, is one of those jobs where the difference between a quick repair and a weekend-long struggle often comes down to having the right leverage and access points. The procedures you are looking at suggest removing the engine or tilting it to access the cylinder heads, which immediately raises the bar for tool requirements beyond standard socket sets.

Your current inventory of wrenches, breaker bars, and a torque wrench is the foundation, but working on overhead cam engines with tight packaging requires specific extraction methods. The decision to tilt the engine rather than removing it entirely is a common trade-off. Removing the engine allows you to drop the heads without fighting suspension geometry or subframe clearance, but it doubles your labor time and introduces risks of dropping the engine onto components like the intake manifold or alternator. Tilt kits allow you to pivot the entire powertrain forward, exposing the head bolts from above while keeping the transmission connected to the drivetrain. If you choose this route, a high-quality tilt kit with a secure locking mechanism is non-negotiable; cheap alternatives often fail under the lateral stress required to free stuck heads.

Accessing the coolant and oil systems during the gasket swap requires more than just a drain pan. You will need a specialized long-reach drain plug wrench for the engine block oil pan, as these plugs are frequently located in deep recesses where standard sockets cannot reach. Without this specific tool, you risk stripping the oil drain plug threads or damaging the surrounding housing while trying to force a socket onto an angled bolt. Similarly, the cylinder head bolts on these Subaru engines are long and require significant torque to stretch properly for sealing. A standard breaker bar is often insufficient because it lacks the leverage arm length needed to apply consistent tension without binding against the engine block ribs. Consider acquiring extension bars designed specifically for the EJ25 head bolt pattern to ensure you can achieve full thread engagement during installation.

Sealant application and gasket positioning demand precision tools that prevent cross-threading or uneven compression. A dedicated torque wrench with a clear, easy-to-read dial is essential here. These engines are sensitive to bolt stretch; under-torquing leads to immediate leaks, while over-torquing can warp the aluminum heads or strip threads in the block. Many mechanics use a printed torque chart alongside their wrench, but having a digital readout or a high-precision analog model reduces human error significantly. Additionally, you will need a set of flat-head screwdrivers with varying tip sizes for scraping old gasket material from the mating surfaces. Avoid using dull or bent blades, as they can gouge the aluminum deck surface, creating low spots that prevent proper head-to-block sealing even if the bolts are torqued correctly.

If your vehicle is high enough off the ground to work underneath without excessive strain, you might consider a transmission jack with rollers rather than standard floor stands for supporting the engine during tilt operations. This provides better stability when shifting weight between the front and rear of the subframe. Finally, ensure you have a reliable way to support the engine once it is tilted or removed; two sturdy jack stands positioned under the oil pan are critical safety equipment that prevent catastrophic failure if a suspension spring fails or a tool slips.
